name: Jamal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say goes out with your name on it. What's a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a 26-tonne rigid with a tail-lift for a drinks distributor. Kegs and cases to pubs, restaurants and corner shops, maybe twenty drops a day. Half the job is driving and half is rolling kegs down into cellars with a rope and a sack truck. I've got a good relationship with most landlords, and the one at the Red Lion gives me a bacon roll on Fridays.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Priya, my girlfriend, in a rented flat near the retail park. She's a receptionist at a dental surgery. Neither of us earns much, and we've got maybe three weeks saved between us. I use AI now and then, mostly to sort out bills or compare phone deals, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, everyone panicked for nothing. I'd probably share a meme about it in the lads' group chat. People like a laugh about that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. Pubs still need kegs and someone's got to get them down the cellar steps. The only thing is pubs keep closing, about one a year on my round, and the distributor keeps squeezing the routes. Money's still tight, and that doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get on the better-paid supermarket trunk runs if a slot opens. Priya and I would keep chipping away at saving for a deposit. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit uneasy about money. Normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your round when a pub closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drop goes, and the route gets merged with someone else's. Last year it meant I lost an hour a day of paid time. That's real money when you're on hourly pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving for a deposit look like right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty a month into an app, when we remember. At this rate we'll own a house when we're sixty. But it's something.

say: I'd say everyone **panicked for nothing** about robots taking driving jobs.
I'd share a **meme** in the lads' group chat for a laugh.
think: The job's fine because **cellar drops** still need a person.
**Pubs closing** and squeezed routes keep money tight.
do: Apply for **supermarket trunk runs** if a better-paid slot opens.
Keep saving **fifty a month** with Priya towards a deposit.
S0.quote: Pubs keep closing, about one a year on my round, and the distributor keeps squeezing the routes.
fieldNote: Jamal's pressure comes from **pub closures** and route merges, not AI.
He lost **an hour a day** of paid time last year, which still stings.
He's content but **thinly cushioned**, with slow deposit saving.

steps.text: Apply for a better-paid supermarket trunk run slot
Keep putting fifty a month into the house deposit app
Keep doing the keg and cellar round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit some jobs harder than others, and drivers are probably in the middle. I'd say people should just learn what they need to and get on with it. That's my line on most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first thing I'd think is Priya. Her job is answering phones and booking appointments, which is exactly what the card says AI takes over. If my girlfriend's dental surgery switches to an AI receptionist, we lose half our income overnight. My route planning would get tighter, but I'd probably keep my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya to start looking now, maybe at the dental nurse course, which is more hands-on. I'd pick up overtime on the Christmas peak to build a bit of cushion. And I'd use the new route app properly once the other lads have worked out the bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly for her. I can cope with my own job changing, but I can't cover the rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise it with Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. She's already a bit worried because the surgery got an online booking system last year. I'd say it over dinner, not like a lecture, just let's have a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if her income drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car payments. We'd sell her car and she'd get the bus. Then the gym, then any holiday. The deposit saving would stop completely.

say: I'd say drivers sit **in the middle** of who gets hit.
People should **learn what they need** and get on with it.
think: **Priya's receptionist job** is exactly what AI takes over first.
Losing her income means losing **half our household** money overnight.
do: Urge Priya to look at a **dental nurse course**.
Work the **Christmas peak** overtime to build a cushion.
Use the new **route app** once others iron out bugs.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for Priya, because he **can't cover rent** alone.
S1.quote: If my girlfriend's dental surgery switches to an AI receptionist, we lose half our income overnight.
fieldNote: Jamal's biggest worry in this picture is his **partner's job**, not his own.
He'd adopt new tools only **after others** test them, as is his habit.
Planned cuts start with **selling a car**, showing how thin they run.

steps.text: Help Priya look into a dental nurse course
Work Christmas peak overtime to build a cushion
Use the distributor's new route app once it's been tested

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal and people should take it seriously, not laugh it off. I'd tell my mates to start saving and thinking now. I'm not going to march about it, but I'd vote for whoever has a sensible plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think: Priya's job goes in 2028 and mine around 2031. That's both of us. The cellar work might buy me a bit longer, because rolling kegs down stairs is awkward for a robot. But not much longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for something more secure right away, maybe a maintenance or electrician course. I'd talk to Priya about moving back near her parents, where rent's cheaper. And I'd save every penny of overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years isn't long, and both of us going at once is the nightmare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which course would you actually pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the cellar engineer one, fixing beer lines and coolers. I already know the cellars, and there'll still be pipes and pumps to fix for a while. A mate from the depot did it and earns more now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years after the AGI. How would you use that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving to pay the bills while I finish the cellar course. By 2031 I'd want to be fixing the beer lines, not delivering the kegs. If I'm still driving then, I've left it too late.

say: I'd tell mates to take it **seriously** and start saving.
I'd **vote** for whoever has a sensible plan.
think: Priya's job goes in **2028** and mine around **2031**.
**Cellar work** buys me a little longer, but not much.
do: Start a **cellar engineer** course straight away.
Discuss moving near **Priya's parents** where rent is cheaper.
feel: **Alarmed** at both of them losing work at once.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd want to be fixing the beer lines, not delivering the kegs.
fieldNote: Jamal sees a **household** hit: his partner first, then himself.
His retraining idea, **cellar engineering**, builds on what he already knows.
He uses the **robot gap** as working time to fund his course.

steps.text: Enrol on a cellar engineer course fixing beer lines and coolers
Move with Priya near her parents to cut rent
Save all overtime pay from the drinks round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people use it. I'd tell the lads at the depot to get a second trade now. Five years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then the robots about 2034. I'd be thirty-four, Priya the same. It's enough time to switch, but we'd both need to start within a year. If we wait, we'll be competing with everyone else who waited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the cellar engineer course part-time next year. Priya would start retraining too, probably as a dental nurse. We'd put the house deposit on hold and use that fifty a month for course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but organised. It's a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is putting the house on hold hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. Priya's mum keeps asking when we're buying. But a house is no good if neither of us has a job to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course doesn't lead anywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least I've tried. I'd rather fail at something than sit on my hands and watch. My dad always said, have two trades if you can.

say: I'd tell the depot drivers to get a **second trade** now.
I'd say there's **time** if people use it.
think: Robots around **2034** leave enough time to switch.
We'd both need to **start within a year** or face crowded competition.
do: Start the **cellar engineer** course part-time next year.
Put the **house deposit** on hold to pay course fees.
Support **Priya** retraining as a dental nurse.
feel: **Worried** but **organised**, with a plan rather than panic.
S3.quote: A house is no good if neither of us has a job to pay for it.
fieldNote: Jamal still expects **both incomes** to go, so the worry stays high.
Five years lets the couple **plan together** instead of scrambling.
He trades the **house deposit** for course fees without much hesitation.

steps.text: Start a part-time cellar engineer course next year
Pause the house deposit and use it for course fees
Back Priya through a dental nurse course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, nobody should panic, but nobody should sleep on it either. That's about as balanced as I get. I'd say it at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2039, I'd have a decent run of driving left. Priya's job is still more at risk, around 2036. We'd have time to save a bit and do courses without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep driving and maybe take one evening course to test the waters. We'd keep saving for the house deposit. I'd watch what the distributor does with new tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for at the distributor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the distributor starts trialling self-driving trucks on the motorway runs, that's my sign. Then I'd step up the course and stop pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd buy the house sooner, while we've both got jobs. Priya wants to get married first, though. We'd probably do both in the next five years.

say: I'd say nobody should **panic** and nobody should **sleep on it**.
I'd say that balanced view at the **depot**.
think: Robots around **2039** leave me a decent run of driving.
**Priya's job** is at risk earlier, around 2036.
do: Keep driving and take one **evening course** to test it.
Watch for **self-driving trials** on the distributor's motorway runs.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, but feeling there's **room to breathe**.
S4.quote: If the distributor starts trialling self-driving trucks on the motorway runs, that's my sign.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Jamal keep **family plans** like marriage and a house.
He picks a clear **warning sign** to trigger action.
Both incomes still end within the decade, so he's **anxious** under the calm.

steps.text: Take one evening course to test a second trade
Keep saving for the house deposit with Priya
Watch for driverless trials before making big changes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Priya and I would both lose our jobs within three years. What would help is cheaper courses for second trades, and some kind of income support while you switch. Not a handout forever, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. Everyone asks about my job, but it's the two jobs together that pay the rent. If you only look at one person, you miss what actually happens to a household.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about my job, but it's the two jobs together that pay the rent.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** drinks delivery driver who rolls kegs into pub cellars.
He rents with his girlfriend Priya, a **dental receptionist**, and they have three weeks saved.
He's **pragmatic**, uses AI now and then, and adopts new tools after others test them.
His biggest fear is **Priya's job** going first, then his own.
In fast scenarios he'd retrain as a **cellar engineer**, building on what he knows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household incomes would go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheaper courses** for second trades and an **income bridge** while switching.
